Going high-tech to save a rare rabbit

By: Jason Boswell | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
going high-tech to save one of the world's rarest rabbits...

Unique Selling Point:
The Riverine Rabbit is one of the rarest mammals on the planet, with some estimates putting the total population at less than 300 individuals remaining. Now a new project involving a specially-trained border collie with a GPS-enabled collar and a state-of-the-art thermal imaging drone is helping to try save this endangered animal.



Summary:
The Karoo. One of the most iconic landscapes in South Africa – a place of extremes, wide, open spaces and endless sunsets. Although the Karoo is well known for its seemingly barren environment, it’s home to an abundance of succulents and interesting wildlife species. One of these is the beautiful, and Critically Endangered, Riverine Rabbit.

Sadly, the much-loved Karoo as we know it is in peril. It’s hard to imagine a South Africa without this backdrop, but threats such as climate change, mining, hydraulic fracturing (fracking), powerlines and the construction of dams are placing this special ecosystem at risk.

The team will use a specially-trained dog and thermal imaging drone to help search out rabbits and work with the farmers to help protect this animal's threatened habitat.

Because the remaining populations live in fragmented pockets of land around Loxton in the Karoo - any developments such as fracking and mining could spell the end for this rare mammal.

We'd interview the expert involved with the dog handler, the drone suppliers and local farmers about this animal's future in this fragile eco-system.

Press Release:


High-tech Rabbiting
The riverine rabbit is one of the rarest mammals on the planet, with less than 300 of them remaining. Now
a new project involving a specially-trained border collie with a GPS-enabled collar and a state-of-the-art
thermal imaging technology is helping to save this endangered animal. Carte Blanche joins the team
working to prevent the total extinction of these elusive creatures.

Script:


Script Visuals
VO: Here in vast expanse of the Nama Karoo…the hunt is on…

On foot through thorny bushes, thick sand and the infamous Karoo heat…

This team is trying to track down an animal so rare, it could disappear before many South Africans even know it exists…

Wide Opening Shots of Karoo, shots of teams searching the landscape

LINK CLIP0922

This is the home of the Riverine Rabbit… one of South Africa’s rarest mammals…in fact it’s so rare that’s its now listed as critically endangered…

Trying to find this rabbit in this vast expanse of land is almost impossible…

VO: Critically endangered is not a term used lightly by conservationists, this means this animal is just one step away from being declared extinct in the wild…

And despite having been declared endangered more than thirty years ago…scientists still struggle to find them…let alone study them…

The last population estimate said there may be fewer than 300 rabbits left…spread across a daunting search area of over 150 000km2 stretching across the Northern and Western Cape…that’s more than eight times the size of the entire Kruger National Park…

The rabbit is so rare and the area so enormous that one of the only ways to film them is through the use of stationary camera traps left out for weeks at time…These few seconds of video is some of the only recorded footage of this animal in the wild…

It’s why this animal has been called one of the invisible species of the Karoo…

But researchers are now stepping things up a notch…Esther Matthews has been hard at work training a special colleague to try track down these secretive little rabbits…
Wide shots of the Karoo, team walking and look exasperated…camera trap footage…set ups of Jessie…
UPSOUND: Esther Matthew

Jessie is my 4 year old border collie she was trained to find BF underground as part of my Master’ Research, and now helping us find RR.

We’re in the final stage of Jessie’s training, which means we’re training in the field by placing scents out in the field and if we see a location where the rabbit jumped up and then she indicates by lying down where the bush where the rabbit jumped up and in that way we’re helping her get a step closer to the rabbit every time…

I think what makes Jessie Special is that from the beginning she was trained to find very difficult species…and hopefully we can eventually use her in collaboration with other techniques as a rapid way of finding the rabbits and finding out how many are left...


VO: And while it’s Jessie’s highly trained nose that’s doing most of the work the team are also trying out some newer techniques… Close up of Jessie sniffing

UPSOUND: Esther Matthew

Jessie will be getting a GPS collar which will help us see how Jessie searches, it’ll be easier for us to mark the locations where she finds rabbits.

So the GPS collar will help us improve the way we work with Jessie…
Graphic overlay of GPS tracking system
VO: One of the reasons the rabbit has been classified as critically endanged is because it’s losing major tracts of its habitat, often due to overgrazing by farmers…the rabbit does prefer the most valuable land, right along the river beds…but Dries Wiese feels the rabbit represents something far more important…
Footage of Sheep in the Karoo and set ups of Dries…
UPSOUND: Dries

This is my land, this is where I want to be, I don’t want to be told one day by my grandkids or great grand kids…listen my grandfather destroyed the habitat of the riverine rabbit.

So I definitely look after my veld and farm…

Question from Mac…

It’s still part of this country, as you and me are part of the country…so if this little animal…this rabbit goes extinct…it’ll be a very sad day… Footage of thermal cameras in the field
VO: In addition to being the home of the riverine rabbit, the Karoo is also the perfect sites for several of the country’s cutting edge astronomy facilities including the famous SKA Project…

And now, the science used to investigate the outer reaches of our universe is finding a new use, much closer to home…

Doctor Steven Longmore and his team of astrophysicists from Liverpool John Moores University are experts in the field of thermal imaging and now they’re turning their attention from the cosmos…to the Karoo…

UPSOUND: Dr Steven Longmore

The power of these cameras is that you can really find the needle in the haystack…

So we’re using thermal cameras which detect heat radition so warm things like you and me glow hot against the cooler background…

For astronmy we’ve been using it for deacdes which is why we can help – but the problem is that these cameras aren’t cheap. It’s only now that they’re becoming cost-effective and can be used in conservation work.

By taking what we’ve learned from looking at outer space and turning our telescope upside down we actually having a really practical benefit to the earth…

VO: While thermal imaging is most effective at night, the cameras are senstitive enough to detect even minute changes in tempratures, even during daylight hours…but it brings it’s own set of challenges…
As you can see it’s very hot out here, and as it warms up the contrast between the warm animals and the ground decreases, so to overcome this we’re going to be working in the early morning before the ground gets a chance to warm up and then again in the early evening when it cools off again…
LINK: So weve been in the Karoo for the past 3.5 hours and we’ve walked over 1.5kms in this vast expanse of land trying to spot the rabbit – but we’re not winning we’re not getting anywhere.

Jessie is going from bush to bush seeing if she can flush it out and get a rare sighting…but we not winning

There’s about 8 people here and we’ve even brought in thermal cameras to try and maybe spot one of these rabbits…but we’re not winning…

However, though the search does continue…
VO: The crew spent days in the field, without so much as a single sighting. ..even with all the advantages of a large technologicaly advanced team…the rabbits remain elusive…

These scans being conducted on foot are just the first step….earlier this year the team conducted field trials in Tanzania… mounting the thermal cameras to drones to cover greater distances and successfully being able to spot small heat signatures in pretty thick bush…

Once permission to operate the drones legally has been granted to the project, the team hopes to apply the same principals to the Riverine Rabbit project here in South Africa…which could help track down these rare mammals….
VO: And while breeding programmes have successfully been used for other endangered species contrary to popular belief these animals actually just don’t breed like rabbits…
UPSOUND: Esther Matthews

They tried to breed them a few years ago, and they were really unsuccessful…some animals don’t do well in captivity it seems that way for the RR.


VO: The animal affectionately known as the Doekvoet has become an icon for the town of Loxton, and for some residents it’s more than just an emblem…

Frieda Hamman belongs to a collective called The Laslappies who produce and sell crafts in and around the town…

UPSOUND: Frieda Hamman

This work is very important to them, as it’s a big challenge…because this rabbit is such a rare species…that can attract tourism.

So that they can generate funds to uplift themselves and uplift the project.



VO: Despite having been listed as endangered as far back as 1986, very little is actually known about this elusive Karoo resident…however, it’s hoped that by bringing in Jessie and these innovative technologies the researchers will be able to learn more and protect this iconic South African species…before it’s too late…



UPSOUND

It’s very difficult to say what the future is for riverine rabbit. We’re hoping it’s not on the verge of being extinct and hoping that Jessie in collaboration with other technology can help us find out more about them to help conserve them, however, with all the development taking place and habitat being degraded…It’s not looking too good for these rabbits but we hope with our efforts we can have a good impact on their population and make sure they keep surviving….



Promos
10 Seconds
1.) UPSOUND – Esther Matthews “From the beginning Jessie was trained to search for difficult animals….

and now she’s tracking the country’s rarest mammal, the elusive riverine rabbit, across the Karoo…

2.) VO: It’s tough going but with good old-fashioned legwork and some out-of-this world technology researchers are hoping to find out more about South Africa’s rarest mammal…the riverine rabbit…

15 seconder

UPSOUND – Esther Matthew, “Jessie is my 4 year old border collie she was trained to find bullfrogs underground as part of my Master’ Research, and now helping us find riverine rabbits…”
Nose to the grindstone, or in this case the ground as the search for riverine rabbit heats up….
